utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are present. I see no absences in the Defence teams except for Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He's working on the issue of experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Madam Nikolic as well is absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Also absent working on other matters. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Prosecution I see Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer and no one else. The witness is already present in the courtroom. And we can continue with his testimony. Witness, good morning to you. Are you receiving interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Welcome back. You are still testifying pursuant to your solemn declaration that you will testify the truth. So Mr. Josse will be proceeding with his cross-examination and then we will see where we stand after that. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When we broke off on Friday, Witness, you had just told the Chamber that you were aware of one attack from within the enclave to the outside in mid-June of 1995. Was that the only attack of its sort that you knew about in 1995, or were there others that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know this from mid-June 1995, the first one. As to the second I really didn't know about that or any others. And I can confirm the one in mid-June. I don't know about any of the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What did you think would happen as a result of these attacks?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at any rate it was realistic to expect a response from the Serb side. And, in the best of cases, with shelling. However, as to the course of events that followed, we saw that what followed was an -- infantry attacks and finally the protective zones were taken control of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'll come back to the attack on the enclave in a few moments' time. Before I do that, I want to ask you about your knowledge of smuggling into the enclave and perhaps the easiest way of dealing with this is to look at 6D27, a document already in evidence. This is a report dated the 31st of December of 1993. And in effect it's an intelligence and security report produced by a -- the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade. And I would like you to have a look at page 2 in your language, page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask that the English be put up in e-court as well, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's being done.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whilst that's being done I think I can continue, because we see that it says that there is information that Avdo Palic is black-marketing cigarettes, weapons and ammunition. Did you have any knowledge of that? To help you and to put it in context, this would have been in 1993, bearing in mind the date on this document.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is the question whether Avdo Palic was included in this criminal undertaking, this black-marketeering?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that. I wouldn't say that Avdo Palic was included in those criminal acts, involved in them. Of course after the arrival of UNPROFOR, well, I don't really know anything about all that. But humanitarian aid did arrive, however, not all the items sent and as was generally the case, not only in Zepa, but in other areas, I assume, as well, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, certain things would enter via UNPROFOR or were brought in in some other way and a system was set up for further distribution and for selling. Now, I really have no knowledge of the fact that Avdo Palic was directly involved in any of that. As far as I know, this was done by other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I see that the English is still not up on the screen, because there is one small part of this document that I would like to read to you, and ask you about.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is on the screen on the English channel. It's not on the channel you can see, it's in the B/C/S for the purpose of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It says, "The former president of the War Presidency of Zepa municipality, Dr. Benjamin Kulovac is reselling medicines, morphine and heroin and is reportedly make some narcotics and hallucinogenic drugs himself." As far as you are aware, is there any truth in that allegation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that. Well, the reselling of medicines, I don't believe that happened nor do I have any knowledge about that, particularly not the second part of sentence that some narcotics and hallucinogenic drugs being dealt with, I don't know. It's incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to the period that I was asking you about a few moments ago and I want you to look at a document dated the 2nd of June, 1995, 6D75. This is a document by Captain Bektic of the command of the 28th Division to the Zepa Brigade. And it gives various instructions. First of all, and I'm summarising, to cover UN check-points and not allow UN troops to cross over to the Serbian side; in case UN troops attempt to leave Zepa, they are to be disarmed and captured and their weapons and hardware put to use in the defence of the territory; assurance to Colonel Dudnik. The fourth point is let him know that we are prepared to defend both ourselves and them in the event of an attack. The fifth point, also use the civilian organs of authority to give him this assurance. Were you aware of the existence of this set of instructions?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time that I see this. I've just read through it, and I think that the way this is written -- well, it's original and valid, I would say, but of course no document which reached Zepa to the military command there, I didn't have an opportunity to see. I heard about some of these things but as I say, this is the first time that I see this. Yes, it was written on the 2nd of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So neither Colonel Palic nor anyone else passed this information on to you, bearing in mind it says that the civil organs should be used to give Colonel Dudnik the appropriate assurance.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Quite certainly, this isn't what he discussed with me or with the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next issue I want to ask you about is the communications centre within the enclave. Prior to the start of hostilities, where did it operate from?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the hostilities dating back to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at first the communications centre was in the same building that I was in. I think it was on the first floor. It was sometime in mid-1994 or the second half of 1994 when it was procured. I think it was 1994, I can't remember exactly. But later on I think that it was moved to another place that wasn't to be its final position, final location, when the attack on Zepa came, it was on Mount Zepa ultimately but I think there was another location which I can't remember just now whether I knew what that was or not, I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'll try and jog your memory in a moment, Witness, but before I do that, bearing in mind you were the communications officer of the brigade itself at one point in time, are you telling the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry to stop you like this, but yes, Mr. Thayer, what is the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I don't believe that that was this witness's testimony, that he was ever the communications officer for the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was put to him. It was put to him from one document in three different places which he said on paper it looks like that in but in reality it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll put it differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Bearing in mind you had some involvement in communications, in relation to the Zepa Brigade, are you telling the Chamber that you don't know where the communications centre was moved from -- I beg your pardon -- to. In other words, you're telling us it was in the farm cooperative building, then you say it ended up in the mountains, but you don't know where it went in the middle period. That's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I wanted to say. I don't remember, perhaps I did know at the time. I know where it ended up. But as to the in-between period, it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The in-between period, it went to the hospital, didn't it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I don't know whether it's to be challenged or not. Let me just say that there isn't a hospital building. What it could have been was to have been the clinic or outpatients' department building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There was -- I'll start again, if I may. Was there a hospital in the centre of Zepa which had one or more patients who actually stayed in that hospital?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat again. In the centre of Zepa, before the war, there were premises which were intended for a clinic or outpatients' department, which is quite different to a hospital. Now, on those premises, I think they were expanded during the war, or rather additional facilities were attached within that outpatients' department or clinic, and in -- to all intents and purposes, a sort of hospital was set up with certain room -- a certain number of rooms and a certain number of beds for patients. That's the real truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I've made the suggestion to you that it was in that place that the communication centre was located. You're saying you don't know whether that's true or not, correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that for a time, well, I don't remember, perhaps I did know at the time. But it's been what, 12 years since then. Well, let's say that that's how it was. I don't really know. But between this time when it was in the building where I was myself, from that time, and to the -- this other period when it was transferred to Mount Zepa, it was somewhere. Now, you claim it was there. I say I am not aware of it. I'm not claiming that it wasn't, but I don't know myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's only fair if you have a little -- a quick look at 6D81, please. This is a document already in evidence. It's a memo from an Alija Gusic, chief of communications of the 285th Zepa Brigade. Item number 5 that I would like you to look at, Witness. I'm not going to read it out, because as I say, it's already in evidence. You can read it for yourself. That seems to suggest, doesn't it, that the communications centre was moved to the hospital basement?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've just read it. And from what I read here, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can you think of any strategic reason as to why the communications centre would be located in the basement of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably the only available space. That's what I assume at least. And it was to some extent protected from the shelling, as it says in this portion that I've just read.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am now going to move on to the course of the negotiations and events as they occurred. And to do that I'm going to take you through a series of documents, primarily in chronological order so that we can try and see how the situation developed. Firstly, could you have a look at 6D104, please. This is a document from the army general staff, signed by General Delic dated the 30th of July. It's to the 1st Corps command, and indeed was intended for the president of the Presidency of BiH. And it says, "We received a report at 0920 hours through our communications system that people have rallied in Zepa, demanding that the president of the War Presidency attend the negotiations with the Chetniks, not to agree anything at these negotiations, but protract them to see if something may be resolved on the international stage. The president of the War Presidency has requested permission to go to the negotiations." Stopping there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, do we have an English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am told -- I certainly have one, and I am told there is one in e-court. We're just checking.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's not been released, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll put one on the ELMO, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Because I see that the assistant...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In fact, I think we've got hard copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And a few of the documents that I'm going to be referring to, translations may only be available in hard copy. We will try to attend to that as I go through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you receive instructions, Witness, to protract the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: The document that we have here is from the 1st Corps -- no. It's from the main command to the presidents -- to the president. Now, I know what I happened over here in Zepa. So the substance of it was as follows: We received the invitation for negotiations on the 12th in the evening. And we had a War Presidency meeting in Zepa in the night well, between the 12th and the 13th of July. That night. And it was -- agreement was required that we could negotiate locally. So this request was probably sent out to the army, to the command, to the General Staff, as well as to the political leadership. Now, a response, we received a response on the 13th, telling us that we could go to the negotiations, and to see what was being offered, what was being put on the table. Now, all this protraction and prolongation was a question of communication between the General Staff of the army and -- Amir and the Presidency. So we were alone there at the time, and this didn't mean much really. Nor did it help in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Interweaving instructions that you may or may not have received with events on the ground, could we have a look at 6D34, which is a document already in evidence. And this is a report from Colonel Palic to a Brigadier Dzambasovic at the army General Staff. And he, Colonel Palic, is talking about the fact that his men were coming under heavy attack, were very tired, and he says, "We are disarming UNPROFOR in accordance with the directive we received earlier." What's that about, please, Witness?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any directives. This was the period from the 13th, although this document is dated the 16th of July, 1995. This was probably communication between the command in the army. This never reached me. I do not have any knowledge of this. This was probably true, according to what is stated here, but I have no comment to make. In that period of time when this was written, I was not in any kind of contact with Avdo, for instance. Or not in any detailed contact. We mostly dealt with UNPROFOR; negotiations, maintenance of communications, so as to find some sort of a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you saying that in those days, around the 16th of July, you didn't speak to Colonel Palic at all?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During those few days before this date, I am almost certain that I didn't. I didn't see him. I was in Zepa, and I think he was dislocated up there on the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, as is clear from this document, he was fighting hard to try and save the enclave being taken by the Serbs, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. That's quite clear, and that was never in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next sentence reads, "I received certain instructions earlier from you too. Everything is going according to plan." I take it from what you already said, you don't know what plan Colonel Palic is talking about?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I don't know. This is a communication that I hear of and see for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would like you next to have a look at 6D107, please. This is a document dated the 18th of July of 1995, from Mr. Izetbegovic to General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does the Chamber have a translation? It does, I am told helpfully by Madam Registrar. Could I say there is clearly a translation error, one that even I can spot. In number 2 the translation says, "500 and 100 volunteers." If one looks at the original document it says, "500-1-000." The Chamber can make of that what they will. But it is -- clearly, as presently translated, it is inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there -- are there any comments on your part, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's clear. Yes. Thank you, Mr. Josse, and thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Here we see that in point number 1 Mr. Izetbegovic says he had been speaking to General Smith, and adds the possibility of an evacuation by UNPROFOR of women, children and the elderly. Point number 2 I want to ask you about. "Perhaps in this case we could insert a brigade or battalion of soldiers to Zepa across the forest path and thus continue the combat with more success. These men from Zepa say that they could find between 500 and --" looks like, "1.000 volunteers." Were you aware of this idea from Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am not aware of this. This is dated the 18th of July, 1995. The fighting in Zepa was at its fiercest at the time. These were probably plans or ideas that our military and political leadership had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the following day you were going to enter into negotiations with the Serb military leadership, how was it that you weren't getting instructions from the Bosniak political leadership?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the negotiation that occurred a day after this document, that is on the 19th of July, that those were negotiations that were not initiated by us. The fighting was ongoing. There was communication with the military and political leaderships, and the following day I didn't have any particular instructions. The fighting stopped, and Mladic asked for the first time that we talk. We weren't sitting around and making plans. This was quite a dramatic and chaotic situation, at least in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm now going to show you a document which details purported instructions from Mr. Izetbegovic to Mr. Hajric, president of the municipality. And this is 6D36. Which is a document dated the 19th of July. I've already said who sent it, who received it. It begins significantly, perhaps, bearing in mind your last answer, "Here are my answers to your questions of last night." And we'll go to item number 3, "My plan: Move out as --" presume that's, "Many civilians as possible. All if possible. The troops stay on and continue to resist. We will do all to help you, one, by supplying MTS; two, volunteers; and three, offensive action in your direction. I believe this is starting today. If we do not succeed in this, you try to push on on those roads. You know which. But now without the burden of women and children who would, in the meantime, be taken out." These are clear instructions, are they not, from the very highest echelon of the Bosniak leadership?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I do not remember receiving any instructions of this kind. This was a communication, I don't know where it ended up or who received this document in Zepa. Was it Mr. Mehmed Hajric or was it just the communications centre? Because this document would first reach the communications centre, which was on Zepa mountain, five or six kilometres away along very hilly terrain, so that each of those documents or instructions, which were not of any significance, would reach the centre of Zepa. So this one is one I don't remember. I don't remember having occasion to see it in Zepa in this period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, let's worry a little less about whether you've actually seen the document. What I'm driving at, Witness, is the suggestion that you were carrying out negotiations as instructed clearly and carefully by Mr. Izetbegovic, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree that there were clear instructions by Mr. Izetbegovic. Even if there were things like this, the situation on the ground was quite different from the way it was seen, shall we say, from Sarajevo. Of course we used all these things more as a device, but unfortunately we were forced to make our decisions mostly on our own. Because our own lives were in question, and the lives of our families.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you recall what time of day it was that you met General Mladic on the 19th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the second half of the day of the 19th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At that time, as far as you were concerned, did you think, genuinely think, that the Zepa Brigade wanted to surrender?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, things are quite clear. To surrender, quite certainly no. Never for a moment did anyone want to surrender. Because we feared for our own lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look briefly, if we may, at some of the things -- conversation between you and Mr. Mladic that day. When I say "you" I mean either you or Mr. Kulovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure whether the transcript of the first video that was played has an e-court number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It does. Could I be assisted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has because in trying to get the transcript before everyone else, we identified that. But it does have. I think 1942.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's P02490, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The first page in the English that I would invite the Chamber to look at, and I think the first page in the B/C/S as well. Probably best not to broadcast this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we scroll down, please. It's the second part of the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We see that Mladic says, "Is there anyone who wants to stay?" You say, "Well, yes." Doctor Kulovac says, "This is what I wanted to tell you, sir. There are people interested in staying." Mladic says, "How many?" And Kulovac says, "What we (unintelligible) through the (unintelligible), that's about 10 complete families, but I personally think that this number could be greater." So at that point in time there was a serious and genuine discussion about certain members of the Bosniak community staying in Zepa, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect that period, probably some local inhabitants, 2 if they had guaranteed safety, that nothing would happen to them, I don't see anything strange in them staying in their own homes and on their own land. I looked a couple of days ago at the testimony, and probably -- not probably, certainly Beno had more information about this because he was more familiar with the local population and what they were thinking at the time. That's as much as I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on with the chain of events, and could we have a look at 6D102. This is a conversation between an Amor Masovic and Zepa itself, timed sometime after 2200 hours on the 20th of July of 1995. Could we scroll down, please. That's fine. We see it says, "You should know that at the negotiations yesterday General Mladic agreed to the evacuation of the civilian population and all military conscripts from Zepa in whatever manner you and Bulajic agree. This is why our side will release 400 of their soldiers from the list of prisoners you have in your possession." As far as you are concerned is that a fair summary of your meeting with Mladic on the 19th of July?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, my memory is now coming back slowly of these things. When we were at that meeting Mladic dictated the conditions, and I think that the last item was that all military-capable men of military age should surrender, et cetera, et cetera. And then we, I think, Mr. Benjamin Kulovac asked whether this could be done, and General Mladic said that there would be an exchange of all for all; all the people of Zepa for all the captured Serb soldiers in prisons over there. And as far as I can remember, things were left at the point when we would contact them to see what our political and military leadership would do to try and find a way for the exchange of the 400 Serb soldiers for all able-bodied men from Zepa. Later, the course and all the activities we engaged in were aimed at putting into effect this idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And to that end you, the negotiators on the ground, presumably had to liaise closely with Sarajevo; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And if I could show you 6D103, which, in fact, chronologically must precede the document I have just shown you. This is a communication from the War Presidency of Zepa to various high-ranking dignitaries within the BiH establishment. It describes -- again, it shouldn't be broadcast, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It describes the negotiations of the day before. We see that in item 1 it says it would allow safe passage across Serbian territory by free choice to the population according to the following schedule, and then it lists those people who would be allowed to leave by free choice. It then deals with the organisation of the transportation. And then it deals with this idea, as you have already told us, about all for all. It mentions in item number 5 the man who was involved in that last conversation we've just looked at, Amor Masovic. It says, "He deals with exchanges on our side." And then I would ask you to note that at the very bottom it says, "The fate of 7.000 people from Zepa, including 2.000 men fit for military service is at stake." So in effect this is you, the War Presidency, setting out what you had agreed and/or asked for at the negotiation with Mladic the day before. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And perhaps I could return briefly to 6D102, please, the second page of that document. We see it says, "The all-for-all agreement reached at the airport on 20th of July includes the release of all members of the army from all of the aggressors' prisons and camps including the new captives from Srebrenica and the release of a number of civilians held by the aggressor in prisons and the evacuation of everyone from Zepa who wishes to go." Two questions: First of all, do you know anything about the negotiations on the 20th of July at the airport?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall now, but I think that I had information in view of the fact that the communications ended up in the communications centre up there, I think I had information -- actually, I did have information that this agreement had been reached. I can't say exactly on what date that was, the 20th, 21st, the 22nd, but as far as I can remember we felt a slight feeling of relief in Zepa. But later it emerged that that was not so, at least that this was not carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My second question is, it's clear from this conversation between Masovic and someone at Zepa, that the understanding was those who wanted to remain in Zepa could do precisely that? It's clear, isn't it, from this conversation.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which conversation? The one before?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The passage that I just read to you and that's on the screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you see it on the screen? Usher, I think he needs --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I can see it. Only the document starting with the words, "The army of BiH at this point in time has a total of," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me read you the relevant bit again.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm reading from the middle of the sentence, "The release of a number of civilians held by the aggressor in prisons," and now the important bit, "and the evacuation of everyone from Zepa who wishes to go."

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I don't know what actually, if someone is living there, living in his own home, and he personally believes that he is safe, and if he wants to stay, I don't see anything strange or -- in it. Yes, that's true. As you say, who wished to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt this chain of documents, and look, because they arise chronologically, at some UN documents dealing with the course of the conflict itself, if we may, Witness. Firstly, could you have a look at 6D87. The documents that you are now going to see, Witness, are English language documents. Could I ask you, do you read English?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can understand English, but I don't think I can really read or translate correctly any sentences of -- that are complicated in any way, so I would request a translation, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely. I just wanted to know that, and any relevant passage, I will read extremely slowly. This is a document dated the 20th of July, it's some sort of UNPROFOR report. It says, by the word "Charlie," "The commander of Bosnian BDE in Zepa, Avdo Palic, announced that if the helicopters with representatives of BHC FWD, UkrBat-1, UNHCR, UNCRC and UNMOs doesn't arrive to Zepa by 21 0800B 95, Bosnians will kill Ukrainians." Did you know anything about that from Colonel Palic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know anything about that, and so I can't comment. All I can say is that it was a very difficult situation, and so possibly some things were -- well, extorted or tried to be arranged with these oral threats. Although I don't know about any physical attacks on any members of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, in that regard let's have a look at 6D91. This is a report the same day, the 20th of July, at 1950, by the looks of it. It says, "Three mortar rounds directly targeted the barracks of UKRCOY. Numerous explosions registered in the UKRCOY enclose. Also UKRCOY camp has been hit with SA and HMG. Origin of fire is ABiH." Do you know anything about that, and is this true?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is very strange, this document. I can't say a hundred per cent, but with great probability, on this date at that -- in that year, in that month, members of the BH Army in Zepa did not have a single mortar round. All I can do is to confirm that I was in the UNPROFOR circle compound and saw with my very own eyes, well, shells were fired from Serb positions. I think it was a PAT weapon that was firing. People in the army know what that is. So that's all I can say about that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 6D92, please. About half an our later, by the looks of it, similar type of report. It says, "ABiH is firing at UKRCOY camp with HMGs. Bosnian soldiers had thrown several grenades into the UKRCOY enclose. Ukrainian personnel took its defensive positions but didn't respond yet. Situation is extremely critical." What do you say about this?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about these occurrences. This is the first time that I hear of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Before I move away from the battle itself and back to the negotiations, could you have a look at 6D82, please, which is already in evidence. This, to be clear to you, is a Serb-generated document from Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric dated the 24th of July, 1995, and it's an intelligence report that deals with events in the battle you have just been talking about. It's quite a long document, but if you look towards the bottom of the first page, it describes, "For four days now the Muslims have been making their presence know with," and goes on then to detail equipment and weaponry, artillery -- of an artillery type, in the possession of the Bosniak defenders. I can see you reading it to yourself. You may want to look at the second page, please, as well, when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm reading the -- do you want me to read the part of the document that's on the screen, or something else? I might not have understood you, where you want me to focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, the part that's on the screen, beginning from, "In any case, for four days now the Muslims have been making their presence known."

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The question is, was Serb intelligence completely wrong when it suggested that the defenders had this sort of equipment at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say. I really -- well, whether this information is correct or whether it is all correct or not, I can't confirm. Probably a part of it is all right, but things that I never fully knew about, I can't comment on now and say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Witness, you must have known what Colonel Palic and his men had at their disposal to defend the enclave. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of it. We knew things in general, as anybody in the enclave knew, that's as far as I knew. But that somebody reported to me and said, "we have this, we have that," no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did you think Colonel Palic was holding out for so long, bearing in mind what the Serbs had at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's -- I'm not contesting that there were weapons, but as to the time, the period, holding out for how long, when you haven't got anywhere else to go, you have to fight. You have to fight as much as you can, as far as you can. So I suppose the situation itself imposed this struggle and how it's described here, and the fact that they held on for so long.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As one of the chief negotiators on behalf of the defenders, surely it was essential that you knew the exact military position?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, did you know the exact military position?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me explain this a little bit. As far as military positions are concerned, everybody in Zepa knew what they were, and the axis of attack came from two sides; the south and let's say the west. Two key axis on the enclave. Now, as far as the situation is concerned itself, it was quite clear to us, to all of us, and this is information from the BH Army command, that it was only a question of time as to how long one could hold out without receiving assistance from outside and holding the lines. It was never a question that this could be done. And, in keeping with this, these activities were undertaken to resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. I'll move back to the negotiations themselves. You saw Mladic again on the 24th of July; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you have already described, and indeed I asked you about it at the start of my cross-examination, the process of evacuation. One thing I failed to ask you then which I would like to ask you now: Is it right that each of the buses was escorted by two members of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember things like that, but most probably that was how it was. Because it was one of our -- well, if I can put it this way, demands, that there should be UNPROFOR members in each of the buses because people felt safer, more secure. So if you have information that that's how it was, then I confirm that that's right. Although, as I say, I didn't see it, but I can't contest it either. I can't say it wasn't so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would now like to turn to the third meeting that you had with Mladic on the 26th of July. And a small part of that meeting was recorded on video and has been played to this Chamber, correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you may recall, and I don't think there's any need to show it again, that there was a man in military fatigues sitting to the left of General Smith, whom you were unable to recognise. Do you recall that from Friday?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. But perhaps it would be a good idea if I were to -- if I were to -- well, if we could have a look at it again for me to be able to confirm it 100 per cent. Could we look at the photograph or the video again?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, yes, I apologise, if I said that I didn't recognise it on Friday, that I didn't recall it, then that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do think that's all right, because as will become apparent in a moment, not a great deal turns on this, save to say that that person, I would suggest, was a Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter, who was the -- General Smith's military attache. He clearly had something to do with General Smith, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. Probably, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Could we have a look at 6D108. This is a document that is not in e-court, Your Honour. It's another UN document, it's only in English, and so I'll need to read parts of it very slowly to the witness. We've got lots of hard copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I invite the members of the Trial Chamber, when they get this document, to remove the last page. Not that I don't want you to see it, it's just it doesn't form part of this document and it will simply confuse. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that the last page I had in my document was indeed the last page, because...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm grateful to Mr. Thayer. He pointed this out to me this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Witness, this is a report, in effect, from Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter. And it's a summary of the meeting that he attended along with General Smith and yourself. Again, it should not be broadcast. In paragraph 2 he says, "At the heart of the situation is the local agreement concluded by local Bosnian officials with the Bosnian Serbs. The agreement is dependent on three things that those who signed cannot deliver. Firstly, that the cease-fire will hold. Secondly, that the Bosnian fighters will lay down their weapons and accept POW status on the basis of a putative POW exchange. Thirdly, that the Bosnian government will accept the conditions for a POW exchange with the Bosnian Serbs." Do you agree with that assessment by Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter that the parties simply couldn't deliver on the agreement?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps the first point with respect to the cease-fire. At least as far as our side was concerned, I don't think that anything was challenged there or that there were any military provocations, or anyway I don't know about them. Now, as to the other two points, to lay down their weapons and the conditions of exchange, in principle I can say that I agree with the assessment made by this person, General, Lieutenant, or whatever he was, that there were problems there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because -- and we could look at the agreement if need be, but perhaps the easiest is that I just read from it. At paragraph 5 it says, "Avdo Palic shall immediately proceed with the disarmament of his units. All weapons from Zepa enclave shall be handed over to representatives of BSA in UNPROFOR's base in Zepa." I'm not blaming you for this, Witness, but it's a fact, isn't it, that when you signed this agreement you knew that wasn't going to happen?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know, and I stated that loud and clear to General Mladic. There's nothing being contested there. So I did not have any efficacious control or influence over the army. When this document, on the 24th, was placed on the table, I said this quite specifically to General Mladic. But they sort of said that will be decided with Avdo, but anyway as far as I was concerned, although I signed the document at that point in time I knew, and I said this clearly, that I could not put it into practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Turning to the -- in fact this is the second page of the document, the exact spot that is on the ELMO at the moment is the one I want to ask you about. This is headed, "The agreement." About seven or eight lines down in that paragraph, talking about Mladic, it says, "He expressed some irritation with the tactics of the government, in particular Minister Muratovic, who he claimed was attempting to misrepresent his position and his good intentions towards the people of Zepa. To emphasise this, he stressed that a doctor, Mr. Kulovac, would leave the pocket with the first medical evacuation and would carry an appeal from the population to the President for the evacuation to take place." Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that Dr. Kulovac, with the first convoy, the convoy with the wounded, went to Sarajevo. Now, as to any possible further talks between Mr. Kulovac, et cetera, I don't know about that. I wasn't in a position to know about that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I want to suggest to you, Witness, that the Bosnian Serbs stuck by their part of the agreement at paragraph 7, and I'll read it slowly, "The civilians from Zepa shall enjoy freedom of choice of place of living and residence in accordance with the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949 and the additional protocols from 1977." Would you agree with my suggestion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be on a separate agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 6D30, Your Honour, if it helps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, so I'm going to go back to Zepa 1995, the 25th of July was the date. The overall situation at that time, well I don't know, actually I don't understand what this means -- well, I'd like to clarify matters and say that people afraid for their lives chose the path that they felt was safer, and that was to leave the area. So I don't see anything in dispute there. Yes, I'm quite sure that people, on the basis of their intuition, felt, and all those who had houses who hadn't been destroyed yet, that had they felt that nothing bad would have happened to them, they would have stayed. But people react according to their feelings and intuition, so that's my answer to this choice of place of residence or living.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs were saying that anyone who wanted to could stay, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'm not claiming that anything bad would have happened to those people, but what I am telling you is why people left Zepa generally. That's it. So I am addressing that second issue, because I know what the emotions were like, and I understand the fear of the people who decided to leave Zepa, and that's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think in fairness to you we should look at paragraph 8 of the document on the screen, remembering that this certainly shouldn't be broadcast. Paragraph 8 on the ELMO, please. Another option, since -- is that the witness be given a hard copy. I think that might make life much easier. Thank you. General Smith explained that on his return to Sarajevo he would meet with Muratovic and wanted to pass on your wishes or concerns, and I'm paraphrasing here for obvious reasons, to the Bosnian government. You stated that the biggest problem in the implementation of the agreement would be the departure of the men of military age from the enclave. So, as you've told us a few moments ago, you made it clear that that was a problem, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At paragraph 9 it says that you emphasised the agreement allowed all males under 18 and those over 55 to leave freely, as well as those who were injured.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. That was never in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At paragraph 10 we see the point that I was asking you about a moment ago. General Smith asked whether anybody wished to remain in the enclave. You replied that the general atmosphere was that everyone would leave on the grounds of security. That you had no details about the handing over of weapons and said that you would have to check that with Palic. You went on to say that if the men in the enclave were more confident that the Bosnian government would agree to the POW exchange, the mood of fear would immediately alter. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everything you've said up to now is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this, Witness: As far as you were concerned, did you believe that the government in Sarajevo were genuine at that point about the all-for-all exchange?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning we did of course believe it. When you have a problem and somebody offers you a solution, you always tend to believe it. It's a sort of psychological thing, psychological aspect. It's what people tend to do. Later on, somewhere around the 26th of July, however, it became clear that nothing would come of that. The promises that were made about these exchanges. So that the events that followed proved that to be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And my last question before the break, when you talk about promises, you mean promises from the government in Sarajevo, don't you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, here. Because this part of the communications with respect to the exchange of able-bodied men was supposed to be led by Minister Muratovic, the then-minister for I think he was relations with foreign organisations in Bosnia. And I've just remembered, looking at this document, that this first meeting was on the 24th of July, at which General Smith attended. And we did have some information, I did at least orally from Avdo, Colonel Avdo Palic, that is, that those negotiations with the Serb side at a higher level, that they were being conducted, and that this should result in a favourable outcome. On our part the negotiations were to be led by Minister Muratovic. Now, from these documents we can see that some meetings were indeed held, but that a final ultimate agreement with the Serb side was never reached on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm content to break now, if the Chamber would like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a 25-minute break, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next document flows directly from what we were just looking at. It's 6D98, and it should not be broadcast. It's a memo or report from the War Presidency, dated the 26th the July of 1995. To Messrs. Izetbegovic and Muratovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It deals with the negotiations at Boksanica which you, Witness, attended. It says three lines down, "Nothing was agreed at these negotiations, because General Smith did not bring the agreement on the all-for-all exchange but today I was informed by the General Staff that the agreement on all-for-all exchange had been accepted by our side and that General Smith had taken it with him." General Smith stated in your presence, Witness, that you, this is presumably the BiH president, were seeking a few more concessions for the exchange to take place. And then a few lines down, "We ask you once again if you have accepted and signed the all-for-all agreement. Please send it overnight to General Smith so that the evacuation method can be discussed tomorrow." It would seem, would it not, from this document, Witness, that you, in the municipal War Presidency, were genuinely hoping at that point that the BiH leadership would agree to the all-for-all exchange?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as can be seen from this document. We sincerely hoped and believed. I remember this meeting on the 26th with General Smith. My memories have been refreshed now, and I had information, as stated in this document, as that is how it was, that agreement had been reached in Sarajevo on an all-for-all exchange. Let me just clarify: In this document there is reference exclusively to the able-bodied men, and at that meeting, at least at the beginning, I was relaxed, as a result of this information. However, General Smith picked up his diary and he said, "No, nothing has been agreed." So that as for these details, whether our side was asking for additional concessions, I don't recall that. Or I don't recall all the details, but in general terms, that is right. We believed and hoped that the agreement would be reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it says in the penultimate sentence, "We repeat that General Smith stated that you had not agreed to the all-for-all exchange and that you had not signed the agreement." When did you first realise that the Sarajevo leadership were not going to agree to an all-for-all exchange and that some other solution had to be sought?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was on the 27th, 26th of July, towards the end of the day. On the 26th I was at Boksanica, I didn't go back to Zepa again, nor did I have any contact with Colonel Palic and other members of the War Presidency. I personally realised this after this meeting with General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And at that point what did you think the military-aged men were going to do, bearing in mind Sarajevo were not agreeable to the all-for-all exchange?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, whatever I were to say would be speculation, because this was a long time ago; 12 years ago. There was a special atmosphere in the air, and it's hard for me to say anything intelligent. I can't say that I thought they would surrender, they would not surrender, they would do this or that I really say that it was on the 26th of July that I realised that nothing would come of that agreement. And then I had no physical or any other kind of contact with anyone from Zepa, including and above all, Colonel Avdo Palic and other members of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In other words, what happened after that point in time was not within your control or personal knowledge; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. So the last meeting with General Smith was on the 26th, and on the 26th, sometime in the afternoon, I reached Boksanica and after that I didn't go back to Zepa, nor did I have any contact, as I have said, with the people and leadership in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 6D89, please. This is another UN document it's a daily sitrep dated the 28th of July and it's page 3 that I would like you to have a look at. It's at the bottom of the page there. On the screen now. It says, "Zepa: The evacuation of displaced people continued. A total of about four to 5.000 displaced people have been evacuated from Zepa to Central Bosnia since 25 July 1995. It seems there are no more people in Zepa to be evacuated. The BiH troops (approximately 1500) remain." That is a fair assessment, is it not, from UNPROFOR that the 1500 people who remained were, in fact, BiH troops?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite a correct assessment, but these were men of the age group from 18, and maybe even under that, from 18 to 55 years of age. To what extent they were involved and engaged during the war, that's another matter. But I'm sure there weren't 1500 who were actually armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then it goes on for completeness, "At 1800B, as a result of negotiations between BiH authorities, BSA General Mladic and UNPROFOR commander, it was agreed that BiH will surrender and give up weapons under UNPROFOR supervision once incident involving security of UN personnel was reported." But that didn't happen, did it?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In conclusion, Witness, what I want to do with the Trial Chamber's permission, is put to you various propositions which amount to the Defence case in this regard. Some of them I accept you have dealt with, and to the extent to which you want to deal with them in the course of the next few minutes is up to you, but bear in mind that some I've already asked you about. The first proposition, I suggest to you, is that the enclave was not demilitarised at all, and I think you've accepted that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree that I said explicitly that it was not demilitarised. In 1993 weapons were handed over, a part of the weaponry, shall we say, to UNPROFOR. And I can say that probably all the weapons were not handed over because quite a number were private property, so people kept these weapons for themselves. Therefore, weapons were partially surrendered, whereas a part still remained in the hands of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next point I want to put to you is this: That the Serbs offered some degree of autonomy, in other words a political solution to the inhabitants of the enclave. I think when I asked you that on Friday, you said you knew nothing of any autonomy-type proposal. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I, and through contacts with anyone, or rather any leader who was in Zepa at the time, these things were not presented to us, nor was I at all aware of it. Whether this happened, who conducted any possible talks, is something I do not know. Therefore, I heard this for the first time in the courtroom here on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next point is that there were attacks from the enclave to Serb targets outside. That I know you accept to some extent. What I want to suggest is that to some extent these attacks were inspired by reason of instructions received from your political and military leadership in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you are referring to attacks from 1993 until the fall of Zepa; is that right? From the enclave? Well, you see, these attacks I don't know about the term "inspired," but they were carried out under the direct command of the 2nd Corps from Tuzla. So there's no question about that. In my understanding, and I'm not the only one in Zepa, those attacks, and I'm speaking exclusively about the attacks carried out in mid-June 1995, those attacks were counter-productive. In military terms they didn't change anything, and they could only provide an alibi to the Serb side to attack, shall we say Zepa in this case. In principle, I personally did not agree with these attacks. I was not alone, but these things were done by the military, because as we were told they were within the system of command and we, as civilians, had no influence over them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As you have just, in effect, conceded, by reason of those attacks the VRS launched a counter-offensive against the enclave; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether those things are directly related, I don't know. But it is a fact that immediately after those attacks, among other things, the attack was launched on the Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There then followed a battle where a fire fight over a number of days between the VRS and the Zepa Brigade, both sides having heavy artillery at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not a soldier so I don't really know what heavy artillery is, but as far as I am aware we in Zepa did not have such heavy artillery. This was mostly infantry weapons that we had. Maybe a couple of those, what do you call them, anti-armour weapons. But tanks or guns, we certainly didn't have in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next proposition I've asked you about already at some length, but let me put it to you shortly. When the negotiations took place, civilians were allowed to remain within the enclave if that is what they wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I clarified this repeatedly, actually what this phrase means, and I will repeat once again. Civilians left Zepa because they were afraid for their lives if they stayed behind. And that is the only reason for their departure. As for the choice of whether they should stay or not, you must admit that in such circumstances it is an issue for each individual. It's not as if one is making a choice to go to this restaurant or another. The situation was quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What I do want to suggest to you in this regard is that a decision was made, from either Sarajevo or locally by the War Presidency or perhaps both, that all the civilians were going to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about any decision from Sarajevo. As far as I am concerned, it is the document I signed on the 24th of July. And I wish to say the following: The situation was such that you couldn't have any influence over any individual when it came to making that choice, and I claim, with full responsibility, that there was no coercion in the sense of forcing everyone to leave Zepa. Because, from the beginning of the evacuation on the 25th, out of fear of boarding buses and crossing territory and Bosnian Serb control, to use those terms, people were afraid of doing that, even. And the actual fact that on the 25th everything was carried out successfully, and there was information received that there was no mistreatment, that everything was successful, then there was a great deal of pressure on the part of the entire civilian population to leave Zepa as soon as possible. So I wish to point out once again that people were informed about the agreement reached, and it was up to each and every one to decide what they would do. All I know is the emotions and fear people felt, if they were to stay behind, and I think the option of staying behind in people's minds did not exist at all at that period of time in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The only problem, Witness, with your reliance in that answer on the agreement, is that, as you have already conceded, you knew full well that the agreement was not going to be honoured by the Bosniak side in relation to the laying down of the weapons. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I am repeating that for the third time. I said that clearly to General Mladic, that neither did I have the authority, nor could I give such an "order." The subsequent course of events showed that there was an attempt to exchange all for all, referring to able-bodied men from Zepa, but at the moment of signing I knew that I had, first of all, no control over this, and from that moment on until the 26th -- even before that, I apologise, from the 19th until the 26th, there were activities being conducted in Sarajevo with a view to finding a solution to this problem and an attempt was made to reach an agreement from the Serbian side for the able-bodied population from Zepa to be exchanged for captured Serb soldiers and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And would you agree that it was part of your tactic, as a negotiator, between the 19th and the 26th, some would say an understandable tactic to try to buy time, firstly to see how the battle on the ground developed and then secondly to try and help out the armed men as best you could? In short you were buying time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly I agree with your statement, but not with respect to a key point. I repeat that on the 19th, even on the 13th, it was clear to us that Zepa could not prevail, and there was no dispute as to whether Zepa would be abandoned. What was disputable was the way in which this would be done. After these negotiations we were more or less sure that for the civilians there shouldn't be any problem with respect to their evacuation. But this tactic that you are referring to related exclusively to the safety and lives of 1500 people of that age group, as described by UNPROFOR. And with regard to this group, there were constant talks regarding this problem between the Serb side, UNPROFOR and our side in Sarajevo. This encouraged us to a certain extent when, on the 25th of July the evacuation started without any strings being attached regarding the surrender of the army. So this tactic related literally only to the way in which people could be pulled out of Zepa alive in a safe manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very near the end now, Witness. We're agreed, everyone's agreed that the civilians were evacuated. So far as the brigade was concerned, it's right, isn't it, that they ultimately abandoned Zepa, still in possession of their weapons?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. I can't talk about the numbers, because all this was happening when I was already in prison, but judging by talk later on, six or seven months later, you hear things from people. But I did get an overall picture as to how this happened. A part of the troops with weapons, that is true, managed to break through Serb territory and reach somewhere around Olovoj and Kladanj, most of them came out there, and a part went to Serbia And were later released or exchanged and allowed to go to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In fact those who made it to Serbia across the Drina were treated as prisoners of war. Did you receive that information?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received that information when I was released from prison. People were talking about this. I know more or less from what I heard from others, what happened. They crossed into Serbia, I don't know how many of them, actually most of them, they were put up in two reception centres, and as far as I can remember most of them before I was exchanged, had the opportunity which they accepted, to go to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think finally this: Would you accept that ultimately the brigade were actually instructed by the BiH leadership not to surrender, and to make good their escape?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, whatever I was to say would be speculating because I wasn't there at the time. Some documents which you may find on an Internet page even refer to some subsequent "instructions" of the military leadership in Sarajevo, the command of the Zepa Brigade. So I wouldn't like to comment on that. Because I know that if you stay behind, and now I'm considering this as a human being, your only goal is to save your live and to go somewhere where you can feel safe. I can imagine how it was for those 1.000 or so men on Zepa mountain. What kind of instructions they received, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, thank you, Mr. Josse. Let's try and review once more the time that have been asked for cross-examination by the other Defence teams. I'll start with you, Madam Fauveau. Do you still require two hours?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I think that I'll need approximately one hour -- one hour 15 to one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Ostojic or Mr. Meek. You had indicated you needed one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that -- I don't think I need to pass on the others because we are talking of minutes. So I suggest, unless there is an agreement amongst you that someone else will go before Madam Fauveau, I suggest that Madam Fauveau proceeds with her cross-examination. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, during your testimony here you told us that you knew that the weapons were delivered to Zepa after the arrival of the UNPROFOR and this by helicopters. Did you know that the weapons were also arriving to Zepa from the land route, from various land routes?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about that. I know about the helicopters; every inhabitant in Zepa knew about those. Let me add to that. Who entered Zepa, well UNPROFOR entered Zepa. They were the only ones. Nobody else entered. So then you can draw your own conclusions from that, who it was who could have supplied those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 5D265, please. And I'm terribly sorry, but I do not have the English translation of this exhibit. Could the witness be shown point 3, it's at the bottom of the page. So would you please scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, can you see this paragraph in which we can see the following: "After training in RNC Bjelevac a group of fighters from Zepa is sent on the 18th of October, 1994 in the direction of Kladanj-Petrovici-Cude-Nevacka, and further on towards Zepa. A group at the strength of 10 fighters and two reconnaissance men from OG6 Istok took the following materiel with them and technical equipment." [Previous translation continues] ... to waste more time, I am not going to ask you to tell us what weapons were brought into Zepa. But as you can see here this document dates from 1996, and, in fact, this is a document stemming from the staff, the Main Staff of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army. Can you see this in the left-hand corner of this document?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the very beginning of the document. Can we just stay with the document for a moment, at the top of it? Can I see the end of the document now, please? Lower down. I think that points 1 and 2 relate to Srebrenica. If I understand what I'm reading correctly. And as for point 3, that is the radio device via which communication was conducted later on. And that device was brought in physically by people on foot. They brought it in.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the second page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But before you look at page 2, is it true say that helicopters were arriving to Zepa until the end of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the beginning of May, I believe. Not the end of May. And when the last one fell, I think that was the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In fact, I don't need the second page of this document. Do you agree that the UNPROFOR forces that were in Zepa knew that the weapons were brought into Zepa via helicopters?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this, you see: Those helicopter arrivals were a spectacular event. The helicopters usually flew at night, after midnight, and there was strong firing at them from Serb positions. And that was always -- well, if I can put it this way, a spectacle. So anybody in the vicinity would have had to have seen it, if nothing more. And in my opinion it is quite illogical that after shooting of that kind, and I'm looking at logics here, that somebody from UNPROFOR shouldn't ask themselves and wonder why the shooting was going on in the first place and what was happening. So if you take a logical approach, although I haven't got information to that effect, they should have known, ought to have known.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But at any rate, according to you, the UNPROFOR never did anything to stop the elicit arrival of weapons into Zepa, did they?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that, no information about that. So I can't say whether UNPROFOR did anything or not, whether it sent out any reports or not. I really don't know, so I can't say. Nor was I in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At any rate the UNPROFOR people did not talk to you, as a representative of a local government, in order to do something so that these helicopters stopped from flying and entering the territory?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with me, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you know that in the month of February, 1995, precisely because these helicopters were flying about and because of the behaviour of the UNPROFOR Serbs had requested that Zepa be declared a non-demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember. Now, if you have any documents or notes about that, it's probably correct. But I personally don't remember that, not looking at it from the passage of time that has elapsed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 5D228, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document stemming from the staff of army of BiH to the Zepa Brigade. Can you see that on top of this document?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see all that. This document, as I say, I'm not familiar with, it says the general staff of the army to the 2nd Corps command. Is it a problem for you to show me the end of the document? Because I assume the conclusions appear at the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: No, there is no problem, but the end of the document is on page 2, and we can see the signature of General Hadzihasanovic. It's not, in fact, his signature, but his name appears on the second page.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, that's fine. I don't need to see it anymore. I had a look. I can't remember, actually, because the document itself is conceived in such a way that it presents reasons to begin with, and then an order follows. So that's what I wanted to read through, and I assume you're going to ask questions about that next. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In fact, what I would like to know is your comments regarding the top page or the top part of the document, above the order, if you could please just show that portion. Can you see the portion in which it is said, "The aggresor on the 16th of February, 1995 presented the demand of UNPROFOR to proclaim Zepa non-demilitarised zone, explaining this by the following reasons: That helicopter flyovers were recorded by which the ABiH brought in weapons and ammunition, that movements were noticed of the BH Army in the Zepa region, and that the UkrBat members were being accused of covering up activities and intentions on the part of the BH Army and could no longer guarantee safety and security and that in the night between the 15th and the 16th of February, 1995, flyovers were noticed of our helicopters and infantry fire was targeting them. On the basis of the above the aggressor informed the UNPROFOR command, sector Sarajevo, that if Zepa --"

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that part. Can we zoom down the document, please. That's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: "That if Zepa is not proclaimed a demilitarised zone, combat operations -- attack combat operations would begin within a period of seven days. The ultimatum dead-line expires on the 23rd of February, 1995."

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be allowed to answer now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The fact that there -- that events were dramatised in February, 1995 or that they were dramatic, I don't remember. I don't remember whether everything ended in communication with Colonel Palic. That's something I am not aware of, I didn't know about that. But I wouldn't agree with the first part, that there were movements, troop movements, BH Army troop movements, I don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In fact, what I would like to know, and what I'm interested in, because you were the president of the Executive Board of Zepa at the time, what I would like you to tell us is, did you know in the month of February of 1995, that an attack would be possible on Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In February 1995 I did not know, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you think that the military authorities of the city of Zepa, would they -- should they have informed you of the fact that there was a military threat, there was a threat of a military attack on Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
